Steelers

Feats of Strength: Rediscovered run game; Derrick Harmon’s heroics key Steelers’ victory over Bengals


Ben Skowronek, Patrick Queen also shine during big AFC North win
By Tim Benz
7 Min Read • Sept. 27, 2026 | 29 seconds ago
Go Ad-Free today
The Steelers’ Derrick Harmon strip-sacks Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow late in the fourth quarter Sunday at Acrisure Stadium. (AP)
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 7:33
Instaread

You can do all the homework in the world on an NFL game, and it can go 180 degrees in the other direction once the ball is kicked.

The Steelers looked like a team that would need three games to score 30 points during the first two weeks. They did exactly that in four quarters Sunday against the Cincinnati Bengals.

The Bengals looked like they had finally built a defense that could be playoff worthy. The Steelers’ anemic rushing attack shoved the ball down Cincy’s throat for 138 yards on 23 attempts.

Both teams entered their matchup at Acrisure Stadium with two of the best pass rushes in the NFL over the first two weeks, and two of the most concerning pass-protection units.

Then both clubs combined for a total of three sacks on 74 dropbacks from the two quarterbacks.

The Bengals looked like the best team in the AFC North during their first two games. The Steelers looked like they might be headed to their first losing season since 2003.

So, naturally, the Steelers won 30-27, and both teams are now 2-1.

How did it happen? Here are the biggest moments, most important momentum swings and some surprising star players in this week’s “Feats of Strength” and “Airing of Grievances.”

—-

Feats of Strength

—-

Harmon the hero: Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow suffered five sacks against Houston last week.

Through 59 minutes of Sunday’s game, Pittsburgh’s high-profile pass rush had none.

That was until Cincinnati’s final possession. The Bengals were on the Steelers’ 38-yard line. They were driving for a potential tying field goal, down 30-27.

That’s when Derrick Harmon made the biggest play of the game with a strip-sack of Joe Burrow.

“Just reading my keys. It was (a) two-minute (drill), so you are thinking pass,” Harmon said. “I saw the right tackle with his foot all the way back. I just knew it was going to be a kick step, and I just went.”

Sebastian Joseph-Day fell on the ball for the recovery. The Steelers took a knee from there to end the game.

—-

Fine first: After a debacle of a first quarter last week in New England, the Steelers had one of their best first quarters in a long time.

Well, offensively anyway.

The Steelers scored two offensive touchdowns in the first quarter. One came on pass from Aaron Rodgers to Roman Wilson.

The other was a catch by Ben Skowronek. That was the first time this franchise has scored at least 14 points in the first quarter since Week 6 of 2019 in Los Angeles against the Chargers.

Defensively, it wasn’t so good. The Steelers allowed an 11-play scoring drive that lasted longer than seven minutes and went 73 yards for a Cincinnati touchdown.

—-

Welcome to the Skow show: Skowronek’s touchdown was big. It was a quick answer for the Steelers offense after the defense allowed the tying touchdown on Cincy’s first drive.

Skowronek also registered a massive fumble recovery of a muffed punt by Cincinnati in the fourth quarter.

Pittsburgh turned that opportunity into a field goal to tie the score 27-27.

—-

Cashing in on a mistake: Perhaps the Bengals’ biggest miscue of the game was roughing punter Cameron Johnston in the third quarter. That occurred on a fourth down from Pittsburgh’s own 41-yard line with just under seven minutes left.

The Steelers made them pay.

The Bengals had kicked a go-ahead field goal to make the score 20-17. With a renewed set of downs — and 15 free yards from the penalty — the Steelers advanced the final 44 yards on seven plays.

Rodgers hit DK Metcalf for a go-ahead touchdown, making the score 24-20.

The touchdown was on a third down. It was the second third-down conversion of the drive.

—-

Return of the run: Pittsburgh’s rush attack was 29th in football through two weeks, totaling just 149 yards. The Bengals rush defense was the third best in football, yielding just 149 yards.

Things flipped this week.

Pittsburgh racked up 138 rushing yards. The club averaged 6 yards per carry. Running back Jaylen Warren went off for 127 yards on the ground. Warren also had an 87-yard run that was called back on a hold against Metcalf.

“During the week, we were all on the same page. That’s what it looks like when we are,” Warren said. “A big part of it was scheme, leverage and taking advantage of it.”

The Steelers changed the starting linemen on the right side. Dylan Cook and Spencer Anderson were benched. Max Iheanachor and Brock Hoffman replaced them in the starting lineup.

That said, a lot of the Steelers’ runs were to the left. But, in general, the offensive line was much better. Hoffman credited coach Mike McCarthy for following through on a promise he made after last week’s loss to New England.

“It all started with our prep. Mike (McCarthy) said during the week he was going to cut down on some of the volume. We were going to get return on investment during the week on the reps we were going to get,” Hoffman said. “I think that is where it started. I think we had a great week of prep. As a unit, we came in and took that loss in New England and said we have to get better. It starts in practice, and that is where our success came from today.”

The pass protection was improved, too. After the Bengals gobbled up eight sacks over two weeks to tie for the NFL lead, Rodgers went down only twice in the game.

—-

Airing of Grievances

—-

Rome wasn’t built in a day: Roman Wilson was getting everyone on his side when he caught his first three passes for 60 yards. That included a 38-yard touchdown.

But then he had one ricochet off his hands in the second quarter. It was picked off by Jordan Battle and nearly returned to midfield with 1minute, 40 seconds left on the clock.

The Bengals turned that drive into a touchdown. It tied the score 17-17 before halftime.

Wilson also failed to haul in a third-down, contested deep ball from Rodgers in the fourth quarter.

—-

What could’ve been: The strike that knotted the score was a deep pass into the end zone from Burrow. Tee Higgins caught it from 28 yards.

Higgins simply outpositioned the smaller Asante Samuel and made a remarkable catch with Samuel draped all over him.

Samuel is (maybe) 5-foot-10, 180 pounds. Higgins is (at least) 6-foot-4, 220 pounds.

Gee, if only the Steelers had a 6-foot-2, 193 pound corner with long arms who could run with a top wide receiver on the rost …

Never mind.

—-

Not as planned: We all knew that the Steelers defensive backs were going to have a hard time matching up with Higgins and Ja’Marr Chase. They combined for 188 yards on 15 catches and a touchdown apiece.

The hope was that the pass rush, which had been quite good the first two weeks, would get home and rattle Burrow.

It did not. Burrow wasn’t sacked until Harmon’s huge game-clinching play.​

The outside linebackers were particularly quiet. T.J. Watt, Jack Sawyer, Alex Highsmith and Nick Herbig combined for just four tackles and one quarterback hit.

If you do want to hand out defensive flowers, though, send a nice arrangement to Patrick Queen’s house. He had 13 tackles, four solo, one for a loss, and he defended a pass.

Your Privacy

We process your data to deliver content or advertisements and measure the delivery of such content or advertisements to extract insights about our website. We share this information with our partners on the basis of consent and legitimate interest. You may exercise your right to consent or object to a legitimate interest, based on a specific purpose below or at a partner level in the link under each purpose. More information

Strictly Necessary Cookies

Always Active

These cookies are necessary for the website to function and cannot be switched off in our systems. They are usually only set in response to actions made by you which amount to a request for services, such as setting your privacy preferences, logging in or filling in forms.    You can set your browser to block or alert you about these cookies, but some parts of the site will not then work. These cookies do not store any personally identifiable information.

Targeting Cookies

These cookies may be set through our site by our advertising partners. They may be used by those companies to build a profile of your interests and show you relevant adverts on other sites.    They do not store directly personal information, but are based on uniquely identifying your browser and internet device. If you do not allow these cookies, you will experience less targeted advertising.

Functional Cookies

These cookies enable the website to provide enhanced functionality and personalisation. They may be set by us or by third party providers whose services we have added to our pages.    If you do not allow these cookies then some or all of these services may not function properly.

Performance Cookies

These cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance of our site. They help us to know which pages are the most and least popular and see how visitors move around the site.    All information these cookies collect is aggregated and therefore anonymous. If you do not allow these cookies we will not know when you have visited our site, and will not be able to monitor its performance.
